title: Hazor and the Northern Kings
summary: Jabin king of Hazor gathers a vast northern coalition with horses and chariots at the waters of Merom. The LORD tells Joshua not to fear, Israel attacks suddenly and routs them, and Joshua hamstrings the horses, burns the chariots, and burns Hazor itself. The chapter then sums up the long war that brought the whole land under Israel's control, including the defeat of the Anakim, and closes with the words that the land had rest from war.
story: Chapter 10 told the fall of the south; chapter 11 tells the fall of the north in the same pattern. A king hears, a coalition forms, the LORD says do not be afraid, Israel wins, and the cities are taken. With this chapter the main fighting of the book is over. The summary in verses 16-23 looks back over everything since the Jordan crossing, and verse 23 announces the transition to the book's second half: Joshua gave the land "as an inheritance to Israel according to the allotments to their tribes." Chapter 12 will list the defeated kings, and chapters 13-21 will describe the division of the land.
historical:
Hazor, at Tell el-Qedah north of the Sea of Galilee, was the largest city in Bronze Age Canaan, with a high upper city and a huge lower enclosure. The narrator's comment that it "was formerly the head of all these kingdoms" (verse 10) fits what is known of it: Hazor is mentioned in texts from the Mesopotamian city of Mari in the eighteenth century BC and in the Amarna letters of the fourteenth century, where its king is one of the powerful rulers of the region. Excavations led by Yigael Yadin in the 1950s and 1960s, and by Amnon Ben-Tor from 1990, uncovered a massive destruction by fire at the end of the Late Bronze Age city, usually dated to the thirteenth century BC. Yadin and Ben-Tor connected that burning with Israel; other archaeologists have proposed Egyptians, rival Canaanites, or an internal revolt. Scholars who date the conquest to the fifteenth century BC look instead to an earlier destruction level.

The list of places stretches across the north: Madon, Shimron, and Achshaph in Galilee; the Arabah south of Chinnereth (the Sea of Galilee); Naphoth-dor on the coast; and the land under Mount Hermon. The "long period of time" in verse 18 can be estimated from Caleb's words in 14:7-10, which suggest the main campaigns lasted about seven years. Judges 4 later mentions another Jabin king of Hazor, which is discussed below.
cultural:
Chariots were the most advanced weapon of the Late Bronze Age, light two-wheeled vehicles drawn by trained horses and used by the elite armies of Egypt and the Canaanite city-states. Israel, a people of the hill country, had none. The LORD's command to hamstring the horses (cut the tendons of their hind legs so they could no longer be used in war) and burn the chariots meant that Israel would not simply adopt the enemy's power. The law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:16 warns against a king multiplying horses, and the Psalms and prophets repeatedly contrast trust in horses and chariots with trust in the LORD.

Verse 13 mentions cities "built on their mounds." Ancient towns were rebuilt again and again on the ruins of earlier ones, slowly raising artificial hills called tells. Israel did not burn these cities (except Hazor) because it would live in them, as Deuteronomy 6:10-11 had promised. The Anakim were a people remembered for their great size, whose presence had terrified the spies forty years before (Numbers 13:28-33). Their survival in Gath is a quiet thread toward Goliath of Gath in 1 Samuel 17.

The repeated statements that Israel spared no one who breathed (verses 11, 14) carry the same moral weight as Jericho and the southern campaign, and Christians have answered them in the same several ways (see the notes on chapters 6 and 10): as God's judgment on Canaan's long-developed sin (Genesis 15:16, Deuteronomy 9:5), limited to that moment and never a license for later war; as the sweeping, stock language of ancient conquest reports, which this same book qualifies when it says much land remained to be taken (13:1); as a stage in Israel's understanding of God read in the light of Christ; and, in a tradition reaching back to Origen, as a figure of the believer's war against sin. Many readers hold more than one of these together.
literary: The chapter mirrors chapter 10 on purpose. The opening, "Now when Jabin king of Hazor heard," echoes 10:1 (and 9:1), and the LORD's word "Do not be afraid of them" repeats 10:8. Verses 1-15 tell the battle and its aftermath; verses 16-23 widen to a summary of the whole conquest. The key word throughout is command: the LORD commanded Moses, Moses commanded Joshua, and Joshua left "nothing undone" (verse 15). The summary also contains the chapter's most difficult theological statement (verse 20) and its most hopeful ending, a sentence of rest that echoes the promise of Deuteronomy 12:10 and is picked up again in Joshua 14:15 and 21:44.

outline.t: Victory at the waters of Merom
Hazor burned and the cities taken
Summary of the conquest and the hardening of hearts
The Anakim defeated and the land at rest

doctrines.note: Against an army "as numerous as the sand on the seashore" with horses and chariots, Israel is told not to fear and then told to destroy the very weapons that might have made it strong. The chapter teaches trust in God rather than in military power.

Verse 20 says it was of the LORD to harden the hearts of the Canaanite kings so that they fought rather than sought peace. God's rule extends even over the choices of his opponents, without erasing their responsibility.
The chapter ends with rest: the land had rest from war. This rest is real but partial, and later Scripture treats it as a foretaste of a deeper rest still to come.

words.note: Iqqer, to hamstring, to cut the leg tendons of an animal. The same act appears when David hamstrings captured chariot horses in 2 Samuel 8:4. It disabled the enemy's chariot force and kept Israel from depending on it.

Merkabah, chariot. The chariot was the tank of the ancient world and the symbol of a kingdom's might. Israel's victory over chariot armies, here and at the Red Sea, displays the LORD's power over the strongest human weapons.

Anaqi, Anakite, one of the Anakim. These were the people whose stature led the ten spies to say Israel looked like grasshoppers beside them (Numbers 13:33). Their defeat reverses the fear that kept the previous generation out of the land.

christ: The chapter ends with rest, and the New Testament explicitly reflects on it. Hebrews 4:8 observes that if Joshua had given the people rest, God would not have spoken later of another day, and it concludes that a Sabbath rest still remains for the people of God. Joshua's rest was real but incomplete: Canaanites remained, and the book's own later chapters show unfinished work. Christians read this as a pattern that points forward to Jesus, the greater Joshua, who offers rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28) and who will finally bring his people into a world without war. The link is typological: the land and its rest are a picture of a greater gift, not a coded prediction.

hard.q: What does it mean that the LORD hardened the Canaanites' hearts, and how does this chapter fit with Judges 4?
hard.a:
Verse 20 recalls the hardening of Pharaoh's heart in Exodus. Interpreters have understood it in different ways. Some emphasize God's direct sovereign action over human hearts; others emphasize that God confirmed a stubbornness already present, handing people over to the course they had chosen, as the kings who heard of the LORD's works chose war while Rahab and Gibeon chose peace. Either way, the text presents the kings as responsible and the judgment as just, and it shows that the path of seeking peace had been open, as Gibeon's example proves.

Judges 4 describes Jabin king of Hazor oppressing Israel generations later. Some scholars take this as a second king with the same name (Jabin may have been a dynastic name, like Pharaoh or Ben-hadad) ruling a rebuilt Hazor. Others think the two accounts preserve different traditions about the same events. The archaeological picture at Hazor is itself debated, so this is best treated as an open question rather than a settled contradiction or a settled harmony.

questions: God told Israel to burn the chariots rather than keep them. What sources of strength or security are you tempted to keep in reserve instead of trusting God?
The ten spies had feared the Anakim; now the Anakim are gone. What fear of yours has God already answered that you still carry?
The land had rest, yet the book goes on to show unfinished work. How do you live with both real rest and unfinished struggle in your own life?
